subject: Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis

messages.author: e808374824de43c9
messages.subject: Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis
parts:
Hey everyone,
I'm pretty new to Stan, and I've been going through the documentation to figure out how to code up a longitudinal factor analysis where the number of time points differs from individual to individual, and the points are unequally spaced. Suppose for example we have two people, the first of whom has two observations, and the second of whom has three. Also suppose that we have 5 outcomes and two factors for each observation. There are two issues I'm not entirely sure how to deal with. Letting i index people, j index time points, k index the outcomes, and p index the factors, (my outcomes are a mix of binaries and counts, so I have to define a custom probability function)

The first is that I'm not sure what is the most reasonable way to declare the outcomes y_ijk and factors f_ijp. I was thinking about defining a single array/vector for all the outcomes using code from the documentation

data {
int<lower=0> N; // # people
int s[J]; // number of records per person
int<lower=0> K; // # of outcomes
int<lower=0> P; // # of factors
vector[N*sum(s)] y; // observations (i don't think this syntax is correct, but hopefully it's clear what I'm trying to accomplish with this)

where y would just be a column vector that looks like

y_111
y_112
.
.
.
y_234
y_235

and then just segment it twice, once to take out all the observations for person 1, and then another time to get the observations for person 1 at time j

model{
  int pos.person;
  int pos.time;
  pos.person <- 1;
  for(i in 1:N){
    pos.time <- 1;
    for(j in 1:s[i]){
      ysub <- segment(segment(y,pos.person,s[i]*K),pos.time,pos.time+K-1) // Vector containing the jth measurement for person i
      increment_log_prob(X) // X is going to be a custom probability function for the entries of ysub which involves the factors and factor loadings
      pos.time <- pos.time + K
    }
    pos.person <- pos.person + s[i]*K
  }
}

I don't think the syntax is completely correct, but the basic idea is just taking all of the outcomes for all of the individuals at all of the time points, stacking them, and then just defining the density on subsets of that vector as per page 145 of the documentation.

I know that if my data were really this simple that I could just define vectors y_11 up to y_23, but my actual data has upwards of 10,000 records and 100 outcomes which is why I'm trying to find another way to do this. So my overall question has 3 parts. 1) Does the above idea for doing this even work at all? 2) If it does work, can I also do this for the factors, i.e. define a gigantic vector of factors and then in the model just specify multivariate normal priors on segments of the vector? 3) If this does work, is there a more efficient way to handle this issue?

My only other issue is that to define the multivariate normal distributions for the factors, I am using gaussian processes to handle the unequal time spacing, and I would like to make use of Kronecker products, but I get the impression that hasn't yet been implemented in Stan. Is defining it element-wise still the go-to option for now?

Thanks in advance

*EDIT* Just a quick clarification, not that this probably matters but I will be using RStan to do this

Martin Flores

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis
parts:
Check out chapter 13 in the 2.9.0 manual on sparse and
ragged data structures (I don't know the chapter number in
earlier version). The key idea is to treat it like
a database rather than a matrix with missing values or
a ragged array. Let us know if you still have questions
after reading through that.

I don't have a reference offhand, but there have been
examples posted of how to most efficiently code Kronecker
products in Stan now.

The problem with defining them directly is that you really
want to use a C++ expression template on the back end and
Eigen, our template library, doesn't support them. I believe
one idea is to code up the compound Kronecker product and
downstream operation, which is most efficient, but can be
combinatorially prohibitive if there are lots of places
Kronecker might be used.

- Bob

messages.author: e808374824de43c9
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis
parts:
I actually have another question regarding this. For the outcomes y, I think that a database type structure would work since conditional on everything else, all the outcomes are independent. But with the factors, I want to use a multivariate gaussian process to handle the unequal spacing between time points, and the way I want to do this is stack the factors for person i at time j into one large vector like this

f_111
f_112
f_121
f_122

and

f_211
f_212
f_221
f_222
f_231
f_232

and then define multivariate normal distributions using sums of Kronecker products. According to the documentation for sparse and ragged data structures, the database structure doesn't allow for vector based density operations, so I think I need to use a ragged data structure for this, which I'm fine with. The problem is that since it's unbalanced data, is it possible to define an array of matrices where the matrices have different sizes? If not, what is the best way to go about defining a distribution like this in Stan? A few things I have thought of

1) Declare one large sum(n_i^2) x sum(n_i^2) matrix Sigma and define N blocks of this matrix and do something like the following

  int pos;
  int<lower=0> N;  // # of observations

int<lower=0> J;  // # of people
  int s[J];               // # of observations for person J 
  pos <- 1
  for(k in 1:K) {
    segment(y, pos, s[k]) ~ multi_normal(zeroes, Sigma[pos:(pos+s[k]), pos:(pos+s[k])])
 }

2) Use a database type structure or ragged array, although I'm not clear as to how this would be done efficiently.

So I guess in summary the question is about declaring N multivariate normals with different sizes. Sorry if this or a similar question has been answered elsewhere, but I wasn't able to find anything about this particular problem. Thanks in advance!

Martin Flores

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Coding up an unbalanced/unequally spaced Longitudinal factor analysis
parts:
I don't know anything about Kronecker products, so others may
want to jump in. These threads tend to stick to whoever answers
first, though, which is why I'm trying to get people to stop
addressing followups to the first person who answered, as polite
as it may seem.

Stan doesn't support ragged arrays directly. You shouldn't
worry about efficiency of data structure manipulation --- it's
basically free compared to all the floating-point arithmetic
and derivative calculations. (It is expensive to declare parameters,
even if they don't seem to be used, as in that block diagnonal
construction for Sigma.)

That's going to be very inefficient to only use the block
diagonals of Sigma. Doing it the more efficient way's going to
be a painful load of indexing, but not impossible. You probably
want to use to_matrix() and store the elements of Sigma in
an array in column-major order.

- Bob
